extracted.intended_audience: recipients of federal education funds (K-12 and postsecondary), Title IX coordinators, school administrators, institutional legal counsel, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory standards from the Department of Education's final Title IX regulations regarding definitions (e.g., complainant, formal complaint), reporting, third-party reporting, consent, burdens, training, and procedural obligations for recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'complainant'
rubrics_metrics.description: Complainant means "an individual who is alleged to be the victim of conduct that could constitute sexual harassment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations revise §106.30 to remove language requiring that the complainant be the person who reported, and to remove the phrase about the Title IX Coordinator filing on the complainant's behalf. The Department explains this wording is intended to be neutral (as opposed to using 'victim' throughout) and to ensure the person alleged to be the victim is treated as a complainant irrespective of who reported the conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third‑party reporting allowed (who may report)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person may report sexual harassment "whether or not the person reporting is the person alleged to be the victim" by using the Title IX Coordinator's listed contact information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department revised §106.8(a) to expressly state that 'any person' may report, including during non-business hours, by phone, email, or mail to the Title IX Coordinator. Third‑party reports trigger a recipient's obligation to respond promptly and meaningfully (including offering supportive measures), but do not necessarily make the reporter the complainant. The person to whom notice must be given to trigger response obligations is the Title IX Coordinator or an official with authority to take corrective action (or any employee in elementary/secondary contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may initiate a grievance process / file a formal complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient is obligated to begin a grievance process (investigate and adjudicate) only where a complainant has filed a formal complaint or a Title IX Coordinator has signed a formal complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other than the Title IX Coordinator (who may sign a formal complaint), third parties cannot file formal complaints. The Department explains this preserves complainant autonomy and avoids investigations when the complainant does not wish to participate; the Coordinator is in a specially trained position to evaluate when initiation is necessary without a complainant's desire to file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX Coordinator / official-to-whom-reporting-must-be-made for 'actual knowledge'
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual knowledge that triggers a recipient's response obligations requires notice to the Title IX Coordinator or an official with authority to take corrective action (or any employee in the elementary/secondary school context).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department revised the definition of 'actual knowledge' in §106.30 to expressly state that 'notice' includes reporting to the Title IX Coordinator as described in §106.8(a). Reports to other employees may not trigger the same obligations except as provided for elementary/secondary school employees. Clear, accessible channels for reporting are required (phone, email, mail, non-business hours).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures must be offered to the complainant
rubrics_metrics.description: When a report triggers a recipient's response obligations, the recipient must promptly offer supportive measures to the person alleged to be the victim (the complainant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive measures are offered to the alleged victim and are not necessarily provided to a third-party reporter. The Department emphasizes that third‑party reporters do not become complainants merely by reporting, and supportive measures are tailored to the complainant's needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parents or guardians may act on behalf of complainants
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.6(g) acknowledges that nothing in the final regulations may be read to derogate any legal right of a parent or guardian to act on behalf of a complainant, respondent, party, or other individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parents/guardians with legal authority may report, consider supportive measures, and file a formal complaint on behalf of a minor or a student with a disability; however, the parent or guardian does not 'become' the complainant — they act on behalf of the complainant. This authority applies throughout the Title IX process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'victim' vs 'complainant' terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations use 'complainant' rather than repeatedly using 'victim' because 'victim' suggests a factual determination that cannot be made until a fair process has reached a determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Clery Act uses 'victim,' the Department explains that 'complainant' more neutrally describes a person alleged to be a victim without prejudging facts. The word 'victim' is used within the definition where appropriate but not throughout the regulations to avoid implying a conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department will not require a federal definition of consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The Assistant Secretary will not require recipients to adopt a particular definition of consent with respect to sexual assault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department believes definitions of consent are best left to recipients (and States) and notes that recipients may consider relevant State laws. The regulations do not impose affirmative consent, 'no means no,' implied consent, or other specific doctrines; recipients retain discretion to define consent for their communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients must define and consistently apply their chosen definition of consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must clearly define consent and must apply that definition consistently — between men and women and between complainant and respondent in any particular grievance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inconsistent application of consent definitions could indicate bias in violation of §106.45(b)(1)(iii) and could constitute impermissible treatment under §106.45(a). Recipients should not vary definitions from one grievance process to the next or apply different meanings to parties in the same process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and evidence collection rests on the recipient
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of a recipient's policy definition of consent, 'the burden of proof and the burden of collecting evidence sufficient to reach a determination regarding responsibility, rest on the recipient' under §106.45(b)(5)(i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations do not permit a recipient to shift that burden to a respondent to prove consent, nor to shift the burden to a complainant to prove absence of consent. Misuse of any consent standard that attempts to shift the burden is not permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative consent not mandated; misuse not permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rules do not mandate an 'affirmative consent' standard, and the Department declines to adopt a federal affirmative-consent requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department recognizes divergent views on affirmative consent; it declines to impose it but also states that to the extent a recipient 'misuses affirmative consent' (or any definition) by applying instructions that the respondent must prove consent, such a practice would not be permitted under §106.45.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rape‑shield protections and relevance of sexual history evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(6)(i)-(ii) deem questions and evidence about a complainant's prior sexual history to be irrelevant with two limited exceptions; the scope of permitted questions/evidence depends in part on the recipient's definition of consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department revised §106.45(b)(1)(iii) to require investigators and decision-makers to be trained on issues of relevance, including how to apply the rape‑shield provisions. While some evidence subject to the rape‑shield may come from a respondent, the recipient retains the obligation to gather and present evidence; the respondent is not required to prove consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training requirements for persons involved in grievance processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX Coordinators, investigators, decision-makers, and any person who facilitates an informal resolution must be trained on how to conduct an investigation and grievance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training must include how to apply a recipient's definition of consent consistently and impartially, how to assess relevance (including rape‑shield rules), and other issues necessary to conducting §106.45 processes in accordance with the regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between general response obligations and grievance process obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations distinguish between a recipient's general obligation to respond promptly and meaningfully to actual knowledge of sexual harassment (including offering supportive measures) and the separate circumstances that obligate a recipient to initiate a grievance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A grievance process is triggered only when a complainant files a formal complaint or when the Title IX Coordinator signs a formal complaint (subject to parental rights where applicable). This preserves complainant autonomy while ensuring meaningful institutional responses to reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respecting complainant autonomy re: Title IX Coordinator signing complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: Removal of the phrase that the Title IX Coordinator may file 'on whose behalf the Title IX Coordinator has filed a formal complaint' clarifies that when a Coordinator signs a formal complaint, that action is not taken 'on behalf of' a complainant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change emphasizes respect for survivor autonomy and clarifies that a Title IX Coordinator's signing of a formal complaint does not place the Coordinator in an adverse position to the respondent or imply the Coordinator can act as the complainant's proxy absent the complainant's consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'elementary and secondary schools' for §§106.44 and 106.45
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department adds a definition aligning with 34 CFR 106.2(k): 'elementary and secondary schools' means a local educational agency (LEA) as defined in the ESEA, a preschool, or a private elementary or secondary school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarification explains which entities are treated as elementary/secondary for purposes of the grievance procedures in §§106.44 and 106.45; the remainder of entities in §106.2(k) are postsecondary institutions.
